cases.name: Molly LaRue
cases.about:
Molly was described as blond and dimpled, quick to smile, solidly built but obviously fit. Spirited. Funny. A blue-haired troll doll dangled from her backpack, and a sunny, energetic artist who in high school had won a national contest to design a 1984 U.S. postage stamp. She had tackled two Outward Bound courses and spent a year providing wilderness therapy to kids in the Arizona desert. As she was hiking the Appalachian Trail, she wrote a poem in a trail log in a Maine lean-to, and signed with her trail name, Nalgene:

 Last evening I whispered “I think there’re less bugs.”
This morning, BRING ON THE SLUGS.
Through the roof of our tent I see their familiar sludge
The stuff that resembles butterscotch fudge.
Squish between my toes in my sandal
Yuck! This is something I just can’t handle.

(Her father) Jim LaRue found comfort in an idea offered by one of Molly’s college friends—that Molly, ever artistic, was now adding her touch to each evening’s sunset. “From that day forward,” he says, “there’s not a day that goes by that I don’t see a spectacular sunset and think: Ah, Molly’s at work.”
cases.narrative:
He tied Molly’s hands behind her back and looped the rope around her neck, and stabbed her eight times in the neck, throat, and back. A hiking couple found her. After a 3-hour hike to the site, detectives found her in the Thelma Marks lean-to, laying face down in a pool of blood.

Not long after, the crew removed the old shelter’s corrugated metal roof, dismantled its log walls, and sawed them up. They burned the wood in a bonfire, scattered the rock foundation. It was an exorcism as much as a demolition. When they finished, nothing remained of the old hut but a bald patch in the forest floor, not even its name. They called the new place the Cove Mountain shelter.
